1.0: QUESTION: Can we achieve complete mathematical certainty in light of Gödel's incompleteness theorems?
1.1: ASSERTS: Gödel's incompleteness theorems destabilized the early 20th-century dream of mathematics as a complete, self-contained formal system
1.2: ASSERTS: Gödel's theorems do not eliminate mathematical certainty—they relocate and constrain it
1.3: REJECTS: Mathematics collapses into skepticism as a result of incompleteness
1.4: ASSERTS: The theorems vindicate a kind of mathematical Platonism—truth appears to transcend formalization
1.5: RESOLVED: Certainty remains in mathematics; omniscience does not
1.1.1: DOCUMENT: First incompleteness theorem shows any consistent formal system powerful enough to express arithmetic contains true statements unprovable within that system
1.1.2: DOCUMENT: Second incompleteness theorem demonstrates no such system can prove its own consistency from within
1.1.3: ASSERTS: These theorems shattered Hilbert's formalist program, which sought to ground all mathematics in finitary, mechanically verifiable proof
1.2.1: ASSERTS: We can achieve certainty about individual proofs—if you've verified a derivation within a formal system, that derivation is certain relative to the axioms
1.2.2: REJECTS: We cannot achieve completeness—mathematical truth outstrips what any single axiomatic system can capture
1.2.3: ASSERTS: There will always be truths we recognize (often through meta-mathematical reasoning) that our formal system cannot reach
1.3.1: ASSERTS: Mathematical knowledge is inherently open-ended—we can always extend systems by adding new axioms, but each extension brings new unprovables
1.3.2: ASSERTS: Mathematical certainty exists as a local rather than global property: certain within frameworks, never absolute across all possible mathematical truth
1.4.1: ASSERTS: The theorems humble foundationalist ambitions
1.4.2: ASSERTS: We navigate mathematics through a plurality of methods: formal proof, semantic intuition, consistency assumptions we cannot fully justify from within
